set.detail:
In 46 the Pompeian cause revived in Further Spain, where the legions of Quintus Cassius' former army mutinied and invited Gnaeus Pompeius, Pompey's elder son, to lead them. With his brother Sextus and Labienus, he raised thirteen legions, many of them Spaniards and former slaves. Caesar arrived in December 46 after a journey of 27 days from Rome. After a winter campaign of sieges, including Ategua, Gnaeus offered battle on 17 March 45 at Munda, on a hill above a plain near modern Osuna or Montilla in Andalusia.

Caesar had eight legions and 8,000 cavalry; the Pompeians thirteen legions, 6,000 cavalry and light troops. The Pompeians held the high ground; Caesar attacked uphill across a stream. The fighting was desperate: the Pompeian soldiers, knowing they could expect no mercy as many were deserters or slaves, fought hard. Caesar's line wavered, and he dismounted, took a shield, and rushed forward, shouting that this would be his last day and their last campaign. He said afterward that he had often fought for victory but at Munda for his life.

The Tenth legion on the right finally broke the Pompeian left. When Labienus moved five cohorts to protect the camp against Bogud's Mauretanian cavalry, the Pompeian infantry thought it was a retreat and broke. The Bellum Hispaniense gives 30,000 Pompeian dead, including Labienus and 3,000 equites, against 1,000 Caesarians. The Caesarians built a rampart of corpses and shields with heads on spears around the town of Munda.

Gnaeus Pompeius fled and was killed a few weeks later; Sextus escaped and continued the struggle for a decade. Munda ended the civil war. Caesar's triumph over Spain in October 45, over fellow citizens, caused resentment.
set.debate: Location of Munda; casualty figures. Location disputed: near Osuna (La Lantejuela), Montilla, or elsewhere in the Campiña; recent finds near Osuna support that area.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
Caesar's dictatorships multiplied: for elections in 49 (eleven days), for a year in 48/47, for ten years, renewed annually, from 46, and finally, probably on 14 or 15 February 44, dictator perpetuo, 'dictator for life'. The title appeared on coins of the moneyers of 44 with his portrait, CAESAR DICT PERPETVO. The dictatorship for life abolished the temporary character that had defined the office since the early Republic and that even Sulla had preserved.

It came with a cascade of honours voted by the Senate in late 45 and early 44: the title parens patriae, a golden chair in the Senate and on the tribunal, a triumphal dress at all times, the right to wear a laurel wreath, statues in all temples and among the kings on the Capitol, the month Quinctilis renamed Iulius, a temple to Caesar's Clemency with Antony as his flamen, his birthday a public holiday, and his person declared sacrosanct. Senators swore to protect him; he dismissed his Spanish bodyguard. When the Senate came to confer honours, he received them seated before the temple of Venus Genetrix, an insult remembered as a cause of his death.

Caesar also controlled elections, naming half the magistrates and recommending the rest; he appointed consuls for the years ahead, as he planned to be absent in the East for three years. When the consul Fabius Maximus died on 31 December 45, he appointed Caninius Rebilus for the remaining hours.

The dictatorship for life made it clear that the Republic would not be restored. Cicero, in his Philippics, called it the source of the tyranny. Within a month Caesar was dead, and in 44 Antony carried a law abolishing the dictatorship forever.
set.debate: Whether Caesar formally assumed the title on 14 or 15 February 44, and whether he sought kingship, are debated.

set.detail:
On 15 March 44 the Senate met in the Curia of Pompey, in the portico of his theatre on the Campus Martius, because the Curia Hostilia was being rebuilt. Some sixty senators had joined the conspiracy, led by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus, both praetors, and including Decimus Brutus, Gaius Trebonius, Servius Sulpicius Galba, Lucius Tillius Cimber, and the brothers Casca. They chose the Ides because Caesar was due to leave for the Parthian war on 18 March.

Omens were reported: the haruspex Spurinna had warned Caesar to beware the danger that would come no later than the Ides; his wife Calpurnia dreamed of holding his murdered body, and the doors of their bedroom flew open. Caesar, unwell, hesitated, but Decimus Brutus persuaded him to attend. On the way, Artemidorus of Cnidus handed him a scroll revealing the plot, which he did not read. Trebonius detained Antony outside.

When Caesar was seated, Tillius Cimber approached as if to petition for his exiled brother and seized his toga. Casca struck first, wounding him in the neck. Caesar fought back, stabbing Casca's arm with his stylus, until he saw Brutus among the assassins; Suetonius records the report that he said in Greek 'kai su, teknon' (you too, child), though he states that Caesar died without a word. Caesar covered his face with his toga and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue, with twenty-three wounds, of which, according to the doctor Antistius, only one, the second in the chest, was fatal.

The senators fled; the assassins marched to the Capitol proclaiming liberty, but the city did not rise for them. The murder led to fourteen more years of civil war and the establishment of monarchy under Caesar's heir. Archaeologists have identified the remains of the Curia of Pompey in the Largo Argentina.

scholarship: Toher, Nicolaus of Damascus: The Life of Augustus (2016)

set.detail:
Two days after the Ides, on 17 March, the Senate met in the temple of Tellus and, at Antony's and Cicero's urging, agreed a compromise: an amnesty for the assassins, while Caesar's acts, including future appointments, were ratified. Caesar's father-in-law Piso insisted that his will be read and that he receive a public funeral. The will, opened at Antony's house, named his great-nephew Gaius Octavius heir to three-quarters of his estate, adopted him as his son, and left 300 sesterces to every citizen and his gardens across the Tiber to the people. Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins, was named among the secondary heirs.

The funeral took place on about 20 March. The body was laid on an ivory couch in a gilded shrine modelled on the temple of Venus Genetrix, in the Forum before the rostra. Antony, as consul, delivered the eulogy: according to Suetonius, he simply had a herald read the Senate's decree voting Caesar all honours and the oath by which senators had sworn to protect him, with a few words of his own. Appian and Plutarch describe a more theatrical performance, in which Antony displayed Caesar's bloodstained toga and a wax effigy showing his twenty-three wounds rotated on a mechanical device.

The crowd, enraged, refused to let the body be burned on the Campus Martius and built a pyre in the Forum from benches, tables and whatever was at hand. Veterans threw their arms on it, musicians and actors their costumes, women their jewellery. Jews of Rome mourned at the pyre for nights. The mob tried to burn the houses of Brutus and Cassius and lynched the poet Helvius Cinna by mistake. The assassins left Rome.

An altar and column were set up at the site, later replaced by the temple of Divus Iulius.
set.debate: The content of Antony's funeral speech is disputed; Suetonius' minimal version contrasts with Appian's and Dio's elaborate ones.

set.detail:
Gaius Octavius, aged eighteen, was at Apollonia in Illyricum studying and waiting to join Caesar's Parthian campaign when news of the murder arrived. His mother Atia and stepfather Lucius Marcius Philippus urged caution, but he sailed to Italy, landing near Brundisium, and learned at Lupiae of the terms of the will. He immediately accepted the inheritance and the name, calling himself Gaius Julius Caesar, and ignored those who urged him to renounce it.

Arriving in Rome in May 44, he declared his acceptance before the urban praetor, Gaius Antonius, the consul's brother. Antony, who controlled Caesar's papers and much of his money, refused to hand over the estate and obstructed the adoption's formal ratification by a lex curiata. Octavian sold his own property and borrowed to pay Caesar's legacies of 300 sesterces to each citizen, winning popular favour. He organised Games of Caesar's Victory in July, during which a comet appeared, interpreted as Caesar's soul ascending to the gods.

Cicero met him at Puteoli in April and wrote that his friends called him Caesar, but Philippus did not, nor would Cicero; he judged him devoted to him. In autumn Octavian raised an illegal private army of 3,000 of Caesar's veterans in Campania by offering 500 denarii each, and two of Antony's legions, the Martia and the Fourth, defected to him.

The acceptance of the name Caesar was the most important decision of the young man's life. It made him the political heir of Caesar to the veterans and the plebs. Though Roman testamentary adoption was disputed in law, the name gave him a claim no rival could match.

In late 44 Antony, as proconsul-designate, demanded that Decimus Brutus hand over Cisalpine Gaul, which a law of June had transferred to Antony; Decimus refused and shut himself in Mutina (Modena) with three legions. Antony besieged him through the winter. In Rome Cicero, in the Philippics, roused the Senate against Antony, who was declared a public enemy in April 43. The new consuls, Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Vibius Pansa, both Caesarians, marched north with the propraetor Octavian, given imperium by the Senate in January.

On 14 April Antony ambushed Pansa's recruits at Forum Gallorum on the Via Aemilia; Pansa was mortally wounded, but Hirtius arrived with veterans and routed Antony's tired troops in the evening. A letter of Servius Galba, one of the participants, to Cicero gives an eyewitness account of the fighting in marshes and woods. On 21 April Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's siege lines at Mutina; Hirtius was killed in the enemy camp, Octavian carried the eagle of a legion when its bearer fell. Antony abandoned the siege and retreated over the Alps with the remnants of his army, joined by Ventidius' three legions.

With both consuls dead, rumours circulated that Octavian had arranged their deaths. The Senate honoured Decimus Brutus with a triumph and gave him command of the consular armies, slighting Octavian, who refused to cooperate with one of his adoptive father's murderers. Cicero's remark that the young man should be 'praised, honoured and removed' (laudandum, ornandum, tollendum) reached Octavian.

The war of Mutina, the Senate's last attempt to assert itself against the Caesarian generals, ended in failure: within months Lepidus and Plancus joined Antony, Octavian marched on Rome for the consulship, and the three formed the triumvirate.

After Mutina, Octavian, denied a triumph and passed over in favour of Decimus Brutus, sent a delegation of 400 centurions to Rome in July 43 demanding the consulship for him, though he was only nineteen, and rewards for his soldiers. When the Senate refused, one centurion threw back his cloak to show his sword: 'If you do not give it, this will.' Octavian then crossed the Rubicon with eight legions, as his father had, and marched on Rome.

The Senate yielded, then reversed when two legions from Africa arrived, then yielded again as the African legions defected. Cicero, who had hoped to guide the young man, went to greet him and received an ironic welcome as the last of his friends. On 19 August 43 Octavian and his cousin Quintus Pedius were elected consuls, an anniversary Augustus would later mark. He took the auspices and saw twelve vultures, as Romulus had.

Octavian's first acts: the lex curiata formally ratifying his adoption, making him Gaius Julius Caesar by law; the lex Pedia establishing a court to try the assassins of Caesar, who were condemned in absence, including Sextus Pompey; payment of his soldiers from the treasury; and revocation of the decrees outlawing Antony and Lepidus.

The consulship opened the way for the meeting at Bononia and the triumvirate. It also showed the young Caesar's ruthlessness: within weeks he abandoned the senatorial cause he had served, while presenting himself as the avenger of his father. Augustus' Res Gestae opens with the claim that he had saved the Republic from domination by a faction, and that the people elected him consul in the same year in which both consuls had fallen.

In late October or early November 43, Antony, Lepidus and Octavian met on a small island in a river near Bononia (Bologna), either the Lavinius (Lavino) or the Rhenus (Reno), each bringing five legions, which they left on opposite banks. Lepidus inspected the island first and waved his cloak to signal safety; the three searched each other for daggers. For two days, from dawn to dusk, they negotiated in full view of their armies.

They agreed to form a board of three men for restoring the Republic, triumviri rei publicae constituendae, for five years, with powers equal to consuls, the right to make laws and appoint magistrates without consulting Senate or people. Octavian would resign his consulship to Ventidius. Provinces were divided: Antony took Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, Lepidus Spain and Narbonensis, Octavian Africa, Sicily and Sardinia, the least secure, as Sextus Pompey controlled the sea. Antony and Octavian would make war on Brutus and Cassius in the East while Lepidus held Italy. Eighteen of the richest Italian cities, among them Capua, Rhegium, Venusia, Beneventum, Nuceria, Ariminum and Vibo, were promised to their soldiers as rewards.

Above all, they agreed to proscribe their enemies, each sacrificing friends or relatives to the others' demands: Antony gave up his uncle Lucius Caesar, Lepidus his brother Paullus, and Octavian Cicero, after two days of resistance. Octavian was betrothed to Clodia, Antony's stepdaughter through Fulvia.

The meeting has been compared to the conference of Luca, but the triumvirate it created was a formal, legal institution, ratified by the lex Titia on 27 November 43. It effectively replaced the Republic's institutions with a junta.
set.debate: The river (Lavinius or Rhenus) and exact date (late October or early November) are uncertain.

set.detail:
On 27 November 43 the tribune Publius Titius proposed a law, carried the same day without the customary interval of three market days (trinundinum), establishing Antony, Lepidus and Octavian as triumviri rei publicae constituendae, 'board of three for setting the state in order', until 31 December 38. The office gave them consular imperium, the right to issue edicts with the force of law, to nominate magistrates for years in advance, to administer justice without appeal, and to allocate provinces. It took effect immediately, the triumvirs entering office on 27 November.

The law legalised the arrangements of Bononia. Its model was Sulla's dictatorship to write laws and settle the state, but shared among three. The triumvirs controlled appointments to magistracies: lists of consuls were fixed for several years, and the consulship became an honour distributed to supporters, with suffect consuls replacing ordinary ones within the year. The Senate was swollen with their partisans to over 1,000 members.

The triumvirate was renewed at Tarentum in 37 for another five years, until the end of 33, though the date of expiry and whether Antony and Octavian continued to hold it after 33 were contested. Lepidus was deposed in 36 after his attempt to take Sicily.

The lex Titia marks the formal end of the free Republic, with constitutional authority vested in three men. Augustus' Res Gestae records that he was triumvir for ten consecutive years. Tacitus, at the opening of the Annals, summarises: Lepidus' and Antony's forces passed to Augustus, who took everything under the name of princeps.

Immediately after Bononia the triumvirs sent orders to Rome for the killing of seventeen prominent men, including Cicero; on their arrival in late November they published an edict, preserved by Appian, explaining that they would rather punish their enemies than be killed by them, as Caesar had been by those he pardoned. Lists followed: Appian gives 300 senators and 2,000 equites, Livy's epitomator 130 senators. Rewards for killing were 100,000 sesterces for a free man and 40,000 and freedom for a slave; heads were displayed on the rostra.

The proscriptions were also a fiscal measure, as the triumvirs needed money for the war against Brutus and Cassius. When sales of confiscated property raised too little, they imposed taxes, including one on 1,400 wealthy women, which Hortensia, daughter of the orator Hortensius, successfully contested in a speech before the triumvirs, the first recorded public speech by a Roman woman.

Appian's Book 4 collects stories of victims and escapes: Antony's uncle Lucius Caesar saved by his sister Julia; Lepidus' brother Paullus allowed to escape; the wife of Quintus Lucretius Vespillo who hid him in the roof; and the woman of the 'Laudatio Turiae', a funerary inscription of a husband to his wife who saved him and confronted Lepidus. Some were betrayed by slaves or relatives, others protected. Thousands fled to Sextus Pompey in Sicily or to Brutus and Cassius.

The proscriptions of 43 surpassed Sulla's in scale. Augustan writers tried to blame Antony and Lepidus, presenting Octavian as reluctant; Suetonius, however, says he proscribed with more severity than the others once he had decided. Their memory shaped the Augustan regime's need to present itself as a restoration of peace and law.

Cicero's name was on the first list of seventeen sent from Bononia, at Antony's insistence; Octavian, after resisting for two days, yielded. Cicero was at his Tusculan villa with his brother Quintus when they heard the news. They set out to join Brutus in Macedonia; Quintus went back for money and was killed with his son. Cicero reached Astura and took ship, but returned to land, seasick and undecided, and went to his villa at Formiae.

On 7 December 43 a band led by the centurion Herennius and the military tribune Popillius Laenas, whom Cicero had once defended on a charge of parricide, found him being carried in a litter through the woods toward the sea. Cicero ordered his slaves to set the litter down, looked his killers in the face, and stretched out his neck from the litter. He was sixty-three. Herennius cut off his head and, on Antony's orders, his hands, which had written the Philippics.

The head and hands were nailed to the rostra in the Forum, where Cicero had spoken. Fulvia, Antony's wife, is said to have pierced his tongue with her hairpin. Popillius received a reward of a million sesterces and set up a portrait of himself with Cicero's head.

Cicero's death became the defining tragedy of the end of the Republic. The elder Seneca preserved accounts of it from Livy, Aufidius Bassus, Cremutius Cordus and Asinius Pollio, and declamations debated whether he should have begged Antony for life. Plutarch tells that years later Augustus found a grandson reading Cicero, took the book, read it at length, and returned it saying: 'A learned man, my child, and a lover of his country.' Octavian made Cicero's son consul in 30, when the decree against Antony's memory was announced.

In 42 Brutus and Cassius, with some nineteen legions and 20,000 cavalry, took up strong positions astride the Via Egnatia west of Philippi in eastern Macedonia: Brutus on the north on hills near the town, Cassius on the south near marshes stretching to the sea, their camps linked by a wall. Their fleet controlled the sea and their supplies came from Thasos. Antony and Octavian arrived with nineteen legions and 13,000 cavalry, short of supplies. Antony, with Octavian ill, camped in the plain opposite Cassius and began building a causeway through the marsh to cut his communications.

On 3 October 42 (some date it late October) Cassius attacked Antony's working parties in the marsh. Antony responded with a direct assault on Cassius' camp, which he took. Simultaneously, Brutus' legions, without orders, attacked and stormed Octavian's camp, where Octavian was absent, having been warned by a dream of his doctor Artorius, or hiding in the marshes, as his enemies said. Each side was thus victorious on one wing and defeated on the other.

Cassius, short-sighted and seeing horsemen approaching, which were in fact Brutus' men sent to inform him of his victory, thought them enemies and believed Brutus defeated. He withdrew to his tent and had his freedman Pindarus kill him; it was his birthday. Brutus wept over his body, calling him the last of the Romans, and had him buried on Thasos lest his funeral demoralise the army.

On the same day the Liberators' fleet destroyed the triumviral reinforcements crossing the Adriatic under Domitius Calvinus. Had Brutus known, he might have waited for the triumvirs to starve. The first battle left Brutus in sole command of a still superior position.
set.debate: The dates of the two battles (3 and 23 October 42, or later) depend on calendar reconstructions.

set.detail:
After the first battle, Brutus held his strong position and refused to fight, intending to starve the triumvirs, whose supplies were running out as winter approached and whose reinforcements had been destroyed at sea. Antony extended his lines southward to cut Brutus off from the sea, and Brutus built forts to match. His officers and soldiers, many of them former Caesarians, grew restless and deserted; his allies pressed for battle. Plutarch says Brutus saw again the apparition that had visited him at Abydos, telling him 'You will see me at Philippi'.

On 23 October 42 Brutus gave battle. The fighting was close and bloody, with few missiles thrown; his left wing gave way and the triumviral legions, led by Antony, broke through and captured the gates of his camp. Octavian's troops took the camp itself. Brutus escaped with four legions to the hills, and that night, finding his men unwilling to continue, he asked his friends to kill him; when they refused, he fell on his sword, held by his friend Strato. He quoted, Plutarch says, a line of Euripides: 'O wretched virtue, you were only a word.'

Antony covered Brutus' body with his purple cloak and sent the ashes to his mother Servilia; Octavian, in Suetonius' account, had the head sent to Rome to be thrown at the feet of Caesar's statue, though it was lost in a storm. Many nobles fell or killed themselves, including Cato's son Marcus, Lucullus' son, and Quintus Hortensius. Survivors joined Sextus Pompey, or surrendered; Messalla Corvinus and the young Horace, a military tribune, made their peace with the victors.

Philippi ended the Liberators' cause and, for many, the Republic. Antony took the East, while Octavian returned to Italy to settle veterans. Philippi was refounded as a colony of veterans.

After Philippi, Octavian returned to Italy to settle some 50,000 veterans on land confiscated from eighteen cities and many individuals, causing widespread hardship and resistance. Antony's brother Lucius Antonius, consul in 41, and Antony's wife Fulvia championed the dispossessed and the propertied Italians, accusing Octavian of exceeding his powers, while also claiming to defend Antony's interests. Fighting broke out in late 41. Lucius, failing to hold Rome, was driven into Perusia (Perugia), a hill town in Etruria, by Octavian's generals Agrippa and Salvidienus, and besieged through the winter.

Octavian surrounded the town with a ditch and wall over fifty stades long and starved it out. Antony's generals in Gaul, Ventidius, Pollio and Plancus, failed to relieve it, uncertain of Antony's wishes. Hundreds of lead sling bullets found at Perugia bear obscene inscriptions aimed at Fulvia, Octavian and Lucius Antonius. Octavian's own verses on Fulvia are quoted by Martial.

Lucius surrendered in February or March 40. Octavian pardoned him and his soldiers, and sent him to govern Spain, but the town council of Perusia was executed, except for one who had voted to honour the murderers of Caesar. Suetonius reports, citing hostile authors, that Octavian sacrificed 300 senators and equites at an altar to Divus Iulius on the Ides of March, the 'arae Perusinae'; he answered pleas for mercy with 'You must die'. The town burned, whether by Octavian's soldiers or a citizen.

The Perusine War nearly provoked open conflict between Antony and Octavian, resolved by the Treaty of Brundisium. It was the low point of Octavian's reputation, remembered in Propertius' elegies 1.21-22, whose author's kinsman died there.
set.debate: Historicity of the 'arae Perusinae' sacrifice. The human sacrifice at the 'Perusine altars' is generally regarded as hostile invention or exaggeration.

set.detail:
In 40, exploiting the triumvirs' divisions and Antony's absence in Egypt, Parthian forces invaded Roman territory under the crown prince Pacorus and Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's general, who had gone to Parthia as an envoy of Brutus and Cassius and stayed after Philippi. Labienus, with former Republican soldiers among the garrisons of Syria, defeated and killed the governor Decidius Saxa, took Apamea and Antioch, and overran Cilicia, Caria and much of Asia Minor, sacking Mylasa and Alabanda, though Stratonicea held out. He struck coins as Q. Labienus Parthicus Imperator.

Pacorus took Syria and Phoenicia, though Tyre resisted, and entered Judaea, where he installed the Hasmonean Antigonus as king and captured Hyrcanus II and Phasael. Herod escaped to Masada, then to Rome. For a short period, Roman power east of the Taurus and in Syria collapsed.

Antony, recalled to Italy by the Perusine War, sent Publius Ventidius Bassus, a self-made man once captured as a child in the Social War and led in Pompeius Strabo's triumph, to deal with the invasion. In 39 Ventidius defeated Labienus in the Taurus and at the Cilician Gates, and Labienus was captured and killed in Cilicia; Ventidius then defeated the Parthian general Pharnapates at the Amanus pass. In 38 at Gindarus he defeated and killed Pacorus.

The invasion revealed the fragility of Roman control in the East and the danger of Roman civil wars spilling into external war. Ventidius became the first Roman to triumph over the Parthians, in November 38.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Bivar, 'The political history of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3.1 (1983)

set.detail:
After the Perusine War, Antony sailed from the East to Italy in summer 40, allied with Sextus Pompey and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, and besieged Brundisium, which refused him entry. Octavian came south with an army. But the veterans of both sides refused to fight, and mediators, Lucius Cocceius Nerva for both, Maecenas for Octavian and Asinius Pollio for Antony, negotiated an agreement in September or October 40. Fulvia's death at Sicyon removed an obstacle.

The empire was divided along a line at Scodra in Illyricum: Antony took the East, Octavian the West, including Gaul, Spain and Illyricum, while Lepidus kept Africa. Italy was shared as a recruiting ground. Antony would fight the Parthians, Octavian Sextus Pompey unless an agreement was made. The alliance was sealed by Antony's marriage to Octavian's sister Octavia, widowed in 40, the Senate waiving the period of mourning; Octavia was pregnant by her first husband at the time.

Antony revealed that Octavian's general Salvidienus Rufus had offered to defect; Octavian had him condemned. Both triumvirs celebrated ovations in Rome, and Antony was given the honour of a flamen of Divus Iulius. The treaty was celebrated on coins showing clasped hands and the heads of Antony and Octavia, and by Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, addressed to Pollio as consul, prophesying a golden age with the birth of a child.

Brundisium averted war and restored the triumvirate's unity, but Sextus Pompey, left out, intensified his blockade of Italy, causing famine and riots in Rome that forced the Treaty of Misenum in 39. The territorial division between East and West foreshadowed the conflict of 32.

In spring 38 Pacorus, the Parthian crown prince, invaded Syria again, crossing the Euphrates. Publius Ventidius Bassus, Antony's legate, who had driven out Labienus and the Parthians the year before, was short of troops, his legions in winter quarters. He used a ruse: through a Parthian sympathiser in his camp, the dynast Channaeus, he leaked false information that the Parthians should cross the Euphrates at Zeugma, the shortest route, which he feared least, so that they took the longer route, giving him time to concentrate.

Ventidius camped on high ground near Gindarus in Cyrrhestica, north-east of Antioch, and let the Parthians approach. Confident after their earlier successes, the Parthian cavalry charged uphill against the camp; Ventidius' legions sallied out and drove them down the slope, while slingers, whom he had deployed specifically against the horse archers, struck with lead bullets, outranging the bows. Pacorus was killed fighting, and the Parthian army broke, losing heavily as it tried to recross the Euphrates. Ventidius sent Pacorus' head around the cities of Syria, which had sympathised with him.

The battle was fought, the sources note, on 9 June, the anniversary of Crassus' defeat at Carrhae fifteen years earlier, which made it a symbolic revenge. Ventidius celebrated a triumph over the Parthians in Rome on 27 November 38, the first ever, and the only one until Trajan's victories, Gellius notes with irony that he had once walked as a captive child in Strabo's triumph.

Pacorus' death devastated his father Orodes II, who abdicated in favour of another son, Phraates IV; Phraates murdered his father and brothers. Antony, arriving, removed Ventidius from command, reportedly jealous, and besieged Samosata.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
Octavian's war against Sextus Pompey, who controlled Sicily, Sardinia and the sea with a fleet manned by many runaway slaves, resumed in 38 after Menodorus' defection. Octavian's fleet was defeated off Cumae and wrecked by a storm at Scyllaeum. Agrippa spent 37 building a new fleet with heavy ships and training 20,000 freed slave rowers in the Portus Julius near Puteoli; he also developed the harpax, a grapnel fired from a catapult to drag enemy ships alongside for boarding. Antony provided 120 ships in exchange for legions at Tarentum.

In July 36 a triple invasion of Sicily began: Octavian from Italy, Lepidus from Africa with twelve legions, and Statilius Taurus from Tarentum. Storms delayed it, and Octavian himself was defeated off Tauromenium, but Agrippa defeated Sextus' fleet off Mylae in August and the land forces established themselves in Sicily.

On 3 September 36 off Naulochus, near the north-eastern tip of Sicily, Agrippa and Sextus fought with about 300 ships each, as both armies watched from the shore. Agrippa's heavier ships and the harpax prevailed: Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and almost all the rest captured or burned, only 17 escaping. Sextus fled to the East, where he was killed by Antony's general Titius at Miletus in 35. His land army in Sicily surrendered to Lepidus, who then tried to claim the island for himself, but his soldiers deserted to Octavian, and Lepidus was stripped of his triumviral powers.

Agrippa received the naval crown, a gold crown with ship's prows. Octavian returned 30,000 slaves to their owners and crucified 6,000 whose owners could not be found. Naulochus secured the western Mediterranean and Italy's grain supply.

In 36 Antony launched the great Parthian expedition that Caesar had planned, with sixteen legions, some 60,000 legionaries, 10,000 Spanish and Gallic cavalry and 30,000 allies, the largest Roman army sent east. Instead of crossing Mesopotamia like Crassus, he marched north through Armenia, whose king Artavasdes II was his ally, to strike at Media Atropatene, an ally of Parthia, aiming at its capital Phraaspa (perhaps Takht-e Soleyman or near Maragheh).

Antony moved ahead with the army, leaving the siege train of 300 wagons, including an 80-foot ram, to follow under Oppius Statianus with two legions. Phraates IV's cavalry destroyed the train and killed 10,000 men; Artavasdes withdrew his cavalry. Antony besieged Phraaspa without siege engines, building earthworks, while Parthian cavalry harried his foragers. Supplies ran low, and an assault failed. Antony decimated the cohorts that fled.

In October, with winter coming, Antony abandoned the siege. The retreat of 300 miles to Armenia took twenty-seven days, guided by a Mardian who knew the hills, under constant Parthian attack; the legions formed the testudo against arrows. Hunger and disease, including poisoning from an unknown plant, struck the army. Antony lost some 24,000 men, a third of his force; Plutarch says he exclaimed 'O the Ten Thousand!' in admiration of Xenophon's retreat. In winter cold in Armenia 8,000 more died. Cleopatra brought supplies and money to the army at Leuce Come near Sidon.

The campaign was a disaster, though Antony avoided Crassus' fate. In Rome Octavian concealed the extent of the defeat while celebrating his victory over Sextus Pompey, and the contrast weakened Antony's prestige.
set.debate: Site of Phraaspa (near Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman); size of Antony's army. The location of Phraaspa (Takht-e Soleyman, Maragheh, or elsewhere) is uncertain; Plutarch's figures likely derive from Dellius' account.

scholarship: Bivar, 'The political history of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3.1 (1983)

set.detail:
In autumn 34, after his capture of Artavasdes of Armenia, Antony celebrated a triumphal procession in Alexandria. A few days later, in the Gymnasium, before a crowd, he and Cleopatra sat on golden thrones on a silver platform, with their children seated on smaller thrones. Antony proclaimed Cleopatra 'Queen of Kings' and Caesarion, whom he declared Caesar's true son, 'King of Kings', ruling Egypt and Cyprus jointly. Alexander Helios, aged six, wearing Median dress and tiara, received Armenia, Media and Parthia, still unconquered. Cleopatra Selene received Cyrenaica and Libya. Ptolemy Philadelphus, two years old, in Macedonian cloak and boots, received Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.

Coins issued at the time showed Antony with ARMENIA DEVICTA and Cleopatra as 'Queen of Kings and of her sons who are kings'. The donations formalised the restoration of much of the old Ptolemaic empire, though most of the territories remained Roman provinces or were held by client kings, and it is unclear what practical effect they had.

In Rome Octavian presented the donations as proof that Antony had become the tool of a foreign queen, giving away Roman territory to her children and claiming Caesarion as Caesar's son, which directly threatened Octavian's own position as Caesar's heir. Antony's dispatch asking the Senate to ratify his acts was suppressed by the consuls of 32, both his supporters, who judged it too damaging.

Modern historians see the donations as a reorganisation of the eastern client system along dynastic lines with Cleopatra at its centre, intended for Greek and Egyptian audiences rather than Roman. They became a central element in Octavian's propaganda campaign of 33-32.
set.debate: The date (autumn 34) and the legal effect of the donations are debated.

set.detail:
Relations between Antony and Octavian broke down in 33, with an exchange of propaganda: Octavian attacked Antony's subservience to Cleopatra, Antony replied that Octavian had deposed Lepidus and kept Sextus Pompey's provinces without sharing, and mocked his ancestry and cowardice. The triumvirate's term expired at the end of 33. On 1 January 32 the consul Gaius Sosius attacked Octavian in the Senate; Octavian returned with armed men and read documents against Antony, and the consuls and over 300 senators fled to Antony in the East.

In early summer 32, at Athens, Antony formally divorced Octavia, sending her a notice to leave his house in Rome, which she did with dignity, taking his children with her. The divorce gave Octavian his casus belli. Lucius Munatius Plancus and his nephew Marcus Titius, who had witnessed Antony's will, defected to Octavian and revealed its contents. Octavian seized the will illegally from the Vestal Virgins and read selected passages to the Senate: Antony had confirmed Caesarion as Caesar's son, made large bequests to his children by Cleopatra, and asked to be buried in Alexandria beside Cleopatra, even if he died in Rome.

The burial clause outraged opinion. Antony was stripped of his consulship for 31 and of his remaining powers. Octavian then organised a sworn oath of loyalty to him by all Italy (tota Italia), followed by the western provinces, demanding him as leader in the war. The Res Gestae records that all Italy swore the oath of its own accord.

The authenticity of the will has been questioned, but most historians accept that Octavian edited rather than forged it. The divorce and the will marked the final rupture and the transformation of a Roman civil war into a war against Egypt.
set.debate: Whether the published will was authentic, edited or forged is debated.

set.detail:
Antony and Cleopatra spent winter 32/31 at Patrae with a fleet of some 500 warships, many very large, and an army of nineteen legions. In spring 31 Agrippa seized Methone and other bases, cutting their supply route from Egypt; Octavian landed in Epirus and camped on the north side of the Gulf of Ambracia, facing Antony's fleet and army on the south side at Actium. Through the summer Antony's position deteriorated: disease, desertion, hunger. Dellius, Amyntas of Galatia and Domitius Ahenobarbus defected. Canidius urged retreat into Macedonia for a land battle; Cleopatra pressed for a naval breakout.

On 2 September 31 Antony's fleet, reduced to about 230 ships after he burned those he could not man, came out of the gulf in three squadrons, with Cleopatra's squadron of 60 in the rear carrying the war chest. Octavian's fleet under Agrippa, about 400 lighter ships, waited in open water. The battle began around noon when the wind shifted. Agrippa extended his line to outflank Antony's right; a gap opened in the centre, and Cleopatra's squadron sailed through it and away to the south, under sail. Antony transferred to a smaller ship and followed her with a few dozen ships. The rest of the fleet fought on until late afternoon; many ships were burned. The army, under Canidius, surrendered a week later.

Plutarch's account, drawing on Augustan sources, presents Cleopatra's flight as treachery or cowardice and Antony's as abandonment of his men. Modern historians suggest the breakout, with the treasury, may have been planned. Losses were relatively small: about 5,000 dead.

Octavian dedicated a victory monument at his camp site, rebuilt the temple of Apollo at Actium, founded Nicopolis, and instituted the Actian games. Augustan poetry, notably Virgil's shield of Aeneas and Horace's Cleopatra ode, made Actium the founding battle of the new order.
set.debate: Was Cleopatra's flight treachery, panic or a planned breakout? Most moderns accept a planned breakout, as Tarn argued. Whether Cleopatra's departure was flight or a planned breakout has been debated since Tarn (1931).

scholarship: Murray and Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)

set.detail:
After Actium, Antony and Cleopatra returned to Egypt. Antony first went to Paraetonium to take over the legions of Cyrenaica, which had defected to Octavian under Pinarius Scarpus, then returned to Alexandria and spent the winter in the 'Inimitable Livers' club, renamed the 'Partners in Death'. Cleopatra tried to send her fleet across the Isthmus of Suez to the Red Sea, but the Nabataeans burned it. Both sent envoys to Octavian; he answered Antony's requests with silence and Cleopatra's with promises if she killed or expelled Antony.

In summer 30 Octavian advanced from Syria via Pelusium, which surrendered, perhaps on Cleopatra's orders, while Cornelius Gallus came from the west and took Paraetonium. On 31 July Antony won a cavalry skirmish near the Hippodrome east of Alexandria. On 1 August his fleet and remaining cavalry went over to Octavian, and his infantry was defeated. Antony, told falsely that Cleopatra had killed herself in her mausoleum, stabbed himself, was carried still alive to the mausoleum, hauled up through a window by Cleopatra and her women, and died in her arms.

Octavian entered Alexandria on 1 August 30, a date later celebrated as a holiday (feriae) at Rome. He addressed the Alexandrians in Greek in the Gymnasium, sparing the city for the sake of its founder Alexander, the god Sarapis, and his teacher Areius. He visited Alexander's tomb, placing a crown on the body, and broke off part of the nose, it was said; he declined to visit the Ptolemies, saying he had come to see a king, not corpses. Caesarion and Antyllus were killed.

The fall of Alexandria ended the civil wars. The Senate decreed that the day was to be a public holiday, and the month Sextilis was later renamed Augustus partly because of it.

After Antony's death, Cleopatra was captured in her mausoleum by Octavian's agents Proculeius and Gallus, who prevented her from burning herself with her treasures. She was allowed to bury Antony. Octavian visited her, she pleaded and tried to win him over, and he promised her kind treatment, but she learned from the Roman officer Cornelius Dolabella that Octavian intended to send her and her children to Rome within three days for his triumph.

On 10 or 12 August 30, she bathed, dined, and sent Octavian a letter asking to be buried with Antony. A peasant brought a basket of figs, said to conceal an asp, an Egyptian cobra. When Octavian's messengers arrived, they found her dead on a golden couch in her royal robes, with her servant Iras dead at her feet and Charmion, dying, arranging her diadem; asked if this was well done, Charmion replied 'Very well, as befits a descendant of so many kings.' She was thirty-nine and had reigned twenty-two years.

Plutarch admits that no one knew the truth: some said she kept the asp in a water jar, others that she used a poisoned hairpin; only two faint punctures were found on her arm, and no snake was found in the room. Octavian, disappointed, had Psylli, snake-charmers, try to suck out the poison. He gave her a royal burial beside Antony, as she wished. In his triumph an effigy of Cleopatra with the asp was carried.

The asp became inseparable from her legend, perhaps because the cobra (uraeus) was the symbol of Egyptian royalty. Horace's ode celebrates her death as noble, 'no humble woman'. She was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom.
set.debate: Method of death (asp or poison) and exact date. The method of her death (asp, poisoned pin, or other poison) is unknown; the date is 10 or 12 August 30.

set.detail:
With Cleopatra dead, Octavian annexed Egypt, though not as an ordinary province. The Res Gestae says simply 'I added Egypt to the empire of the Roman people.' Egypt was governed not by a senator but by an equestrian prefect, the praefectus Alexandreae et Aegypti, appointed by and responsible to Octavian personally, the first being Gaius Cornelius Gallus. Senators and leading equites were forbidden to enter Egypt without the emperor's permission, because whoever held it, with its grain and strategic position, could starve Italy. Three legions were stationed there.

The administrative structure of the Ptolemies was largely retained: the nomes, the bureaucracy, the royal land and monopolies, and the Greek language of administration. Octavian appeared as pharaoh in temple reliefs, with Egyptian titles, though he never visited Egypt again. The treasure of the Ptolemies paid off his soldiers, and Roman interest rates fell from 12 to 4 per cent, Dio says, because of the influx of money.

Egypt's annual grain shipment, perhaps a third of Rome's needs under the empire, made it central to the city's supply. Octavian had the irrigation canals cleared by the army. The prefect Gallus campaigned in Upper Egypt, suppressed a revolt in the Thebaid, and set up a boastful trilingual stele at Philae; his self-glorification led to his disgrace and suicide in 27/26.

The anniversary of the capture of Alexandria (1 August) was celebrated, and in Egypt the years were counted from Octavian's conquest. The Augustan regime presented the conquest as the end of the civil wars. Egypt remained under Roman and then Byzantine rule until the Arab conquest of 641.

scholarship: Capponi, Augustan Egypt: The Creation of a Roman Province (2005)

set.detail:
On 13, 14 and 15 August 29, Octavian celebrated three triumphs: for Illyricum (his campaigns of 35-33), for Actium, and for Egypt. The third was the most splendid. Effigies of Cleopatra on a couch with an asp were carried, and her children by Antony, Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene, walked in the procession. The Egyptian treasure was so vast that it lowered interest rates and raised land prices. Each soldier received 1,000 sesterces and each citizen 400. Octavian rode in the triumphal chariot with his stepson Tiberius and nephew Marcellus on the trace horses.

Unusually, the magistrates and the Senate followed the chariot rather than leading it, a break with tradition that marked Octavian's supremacy. On 18 August he dedicated the temple of Divus Iulius in the Forum, adorned with the rams of ships from Actium, and on 28 August the Curia Julia with the statue and altar of Victory, which had been brought from Tarentum. Games followed, including a Troy game by aristocratic boys and gladiatorial combats with Dacians and Suebi.

Octavian also closed the doors of the temple of Janus for the first time since 235, signifying peace throughout the empire. The Senate voted many honours: an arch at Brundisium and in the Forum, his name in the hymn of the Salii, and his birthday as a holiday.

The triple triumph marked the formal end of the civil wars and the beginning of the transition to the Principate. Virgil, in the Aeneid, placed the triumph at the climax of the shield of Aeneas, with Octavian receiving the gifts of the nations at the temple of Apollo. The settlement of 27 followed.

On 13 January 27 Octavian, consul for the seventh time, appeared before the Senate and announced that he was returning all his powers, provinces and armies to the Senate and people, restoring the Republic (res publica restituta). The Senate, after a show of protest, persuaded him to accept a large provincial command for ten years: Spain, Gaul and Syria, with Cyprus and Egypt, which held most of the legions. The remaining provinces were governed by proconsuls chosen by lot from among senators. He was to govern his provinces through legates of his choosing, as Pompey had governed Spain in 55-50.

On 16 January the Senate voted him new honours: the name Augustus, proposed by Munatius Plancus, with its religious associations (augur, augere); a golden shield in the Curia inscribed with his virtues of courage, clemency, justice and piety (the clupeus virtutis, a copy of which survives from Arles); laurel trees flanking his door and the civic crown of oak leaves over it, for saving citizens. He also continued to hold the consulship each year until 23.

The settlement was the founding act of the Principate. Augustus' own account in the Res Gestae claims that after this he surpassed all in authority (auctoritas) but had no more power than his colleagues in each magistracy. Tacitus and Dio saw it as monarchy under a republican veneer. The settlement was revised in 23, when Augustus resigned the consulship and received tribunician power and imperium maius.

Modern historians debate how far the settlement represented genuine power-sharing. Syme saw it as a facade; others (Millar, Lange) emphasise the continuities with triumviral and republican practice. Coins of 28 proclaim him 'champion of the liberty of the Roman people', and a gold aureus of 28 shows him restoring 'laws and rights to the Roman people'.

On 16 January 27, three days after Octavian's formal restoration of the Republic, the Senate, on the motion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, voted that he be called Augustus. Some had proposed Romulus, as the second founder of Rome, but this was rejected, Suetonius says, because of Romulus' associations with kingship and fratricide. Augustus was a word of religious solemnity, used of holy places and things consecrated by augury. Ennius had written that Rome was founded 'augusto augurio', with august augury. The name implied that its bearer was more than human without claiming divinity.

The full name was now Imperator Caesar Divi filius Augustus: Imperator as a first name, an innovation emphasising military victory; Caesar as a family name; son of the deified Julius; and Augustus as a cognomen. Ovid's Fasti explains that the sacred things are called august, as are temples consecrated by priests, and that the word shares its root with augere, to increase.

Dio says the name signified something more than human, and that it was a title of honour rather than power. The month Sextilis, in which he had won his first consulship and conquered Egypt, was renamed Augustus in 8 BC. The name became the title of all subsequent emperors, and in Greek Sebastos, 'the revered one'.

The choice of 'Augustus' over 'Romulus' shows the care with which Octavian shaped his public identity. It distanced him from the bloodstained triumvir and from kingship, while giving him a unique and sacred standing. The name is the beginning of the imperial titulature.

Rome's first war of conquest beyond the Alps grew out of its alliance with Massalia, the Greek city whose territory was harried by the Celto-Ligurian Salluvii (Salyes). In 125 the consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus answered Massalia's appeal and defeated the Salluvii; his successor Gaius Sextius Calvinus (124-122) destroyed their oppidum at Entremont and founded a garrison at the hot springs that became Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), the first Roman settlement in Gaul.

The Salluvian king Teutomalius fled to the Allobroges, a powerful people between the Rhône and the Isère, who refused to surrender him and who also attacked the Aedui, recently recognised as 'brothers and kinsmen' of the Roman people. In 121 Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium near the confluence of the Sorgue and the Rhône, using war elephants that terrified the Gauls. Later that year the consul Quintus Fabius Maximus, grandson of Aemilius Paullus, defeated the combined Allobroges and Arverni under their king Bituitus at the confluence of the Isère and Rhône; the ancient figure of 120,000 Gallic dead is fantastic, but the victory was decisive. Bituitus, lured to Domitius for negotiations, was arrested and sent to Rome, where he walked in Fabius' triumph in his silver armour, then interned at Alba Fucens.

Fabius took the cognomen Allobrogicus and built the Fornix Fabianus in the Forum; Domitius rode an elephant through the province and set up trophies. The Allobroges were annexed, the Arverni left free. Domitius built the Via Domitia linking Italy to Spain, and in 118 the colony of Narbo Martius was founded against senatorial opposition. The territory, called simply 'the Province' (hence Provence), became Gallia Transalpina, later Narbonensis.

The war secured the land route to Spain and made Rome a power in Gaul two generations before Caesar. Its new province bore the brunt of the Cimbric invasions a decade later.
set.debate: The dates of the battles of Vindalium and the Isara (both 121) and the founding of the province are debated.

scholarship: Ebel, Transalpine Gaul: The Emergence of a Roman Province (1976)

set.detail:
The Jugurthine War arose from the succession crisis in Numidia after Micipsa's death in 118, when Jugurtha, adopted nephew of the old king and a veteran of Numantia with Roman friends, killed his cousin Hiempsal and drove out Adherbal. The Senate divided the kingdom in 116, but in 112 Jugurtha besieged Adherbal at Cirta and massacred the Italian traders who had defended it. Under pressure from the tribune Gaius Memmius and the equites, Rome declared war in 111.

The first phase was marked by failure and scandal. The consul Calpurnius Bestia accepted Jugurtha's nominal surrender in 111; Jugurtha, summoned to Rome as a witness, had a rival, Massiva, murdered in the city, and left saying Rome was a city for sale. In 110 Aulus Postumius Albinus' army was trapped at Suthul and sent under the yoke. The Mamilian commission of 109 condemned Opimius, Bestia and others for corruption.

Quintus Caecilius Metellus (109-107) restored discipline, won the battle of the Muthul, and took Thala, but could not catch Jugurtha, whose guerrilla war exploited Numidia's steppes and fortresses. His legate Gaius Marius won the consulship of 107 by promising a quick victory, recruited the capite censi, and campaigned deep into the south, capturing Capsa and a royal treasure fort on the Mulucha. Jugurtha allied with his father-in-law Bocchus I of Mauretania; their combined armies nearly defeated Marius near Cirta in 106. Finally Marius' quaestor Sulla persuaded Bocchus to betray Jugurtha in 105.

Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum makes the war a study of senatorial corruption and the rise of the new man; modern historians are more sceptical, stressing the logistical difficulties. Its political legacy was immense: it made Marius, introduced Sulla, and began their enmity.

scholarship: Morstein-Marx, 'The myth of Numidian origins in Sallust', AJPh 122 (2001)

set.detail:
The Cimbri, a people from Jutland, and the Teutones, joined by the Ambrones and Helvetian groups (Tigurini, Tougeni), migrated south about 120, perhaps after storm floods, wandering through central Europe. In 113 they reached Noricum, a Roman friend, and the consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo attacked them treacherously at Noreia and was badly defeated. They moved west into Gaul, and asked Rome for land in return for service; refused, they defeated Silanus in 109, the Tigurini killed the consul Lucius Cassius Longinus near Burdigala in 107, and in 105 the Germans annihilated the armies of Caepio and Mallius Maximus at Arausio, with the sources claiming 80,000 Roman dead.

Rome expected invasion of Italy. The people elected Marius to five consecutive consulships (104-100). Fortunately the Cimbri turned to Spain, where the Celtiberians repulsed them, and the Teutones roamed northern Gaul, giving Marius two years to train his army in the Rhône valley. In 102 the invaders divided. Marius destroyed the Ambrones and Teutones at Aquae Sextiae. The Cimbri crossed the Brenner, drove Catulus back from the Adige, and wintered in the Po plain; in 101 Marius and Catulus annihilated them on the Raudine Plain near Vercellae.

The war was the gravest threat to Italy since Hannibal, and in Roman memory it revived the terror of the Gallic sack of 390. It transformed the Roman army: the levy of the capite censi, professional training, the eagle as legionary standard. Politically, it established the precedent of repeated consulships for a saviour general, and Marius' hold on popular favour.

Captive Cimbri and Teutones were sold as slaves; some may have fought for Spartacus. Caesar's later war in Gaul was presented in part as preventing another such invasion, and Caesar claimed the Atuatuci were descended from Cimbric survivors.
set.debate: The causes of the migration and the size of the groups are unknown; ancient figures are exaggerated.

scholarship: Evans, 'Rome's Cimbric Wars (114-101 BC) and their impact on the Iberian peninsula', Acta Classica 48 (2005)

set.detail:
The Second Sicilian Slave War began in 104, triggered indirectly by the Cimbric war. When Marius asked allied kings for troops, Nicomedes III of Bithynia replied that most of his men had been carried off as slaves by Roman tax-farmers. The Senate decreed that free allies held as slaves in the provinces be freed. In Sicily the governor Publius Licinius Nerva freed 800 in a few days, then, under pressure from the slaveowners, stopped. The disappointed slaves rose.

In eastern Sicily the slaves chose Salvius, a soothsayer and flute-player, as king; he took the royal name Tryphon, after the Seleucid usurper, and built a capital at Triocala in the west. In the west another revolt was led by Athenion, a Cilician slave estate manager and astrologer. They combined forces, perhaps 40,000 men, and the revolt spread over most of the island; cities were besieged and the countryside ravaged, causing famine. Nerva and his successor Lucius Licinius Lucullus failed to end it; Lucullus won a battle at Scirthaea in 103 but could not take Triocala, and both governors were later convicted. Tryphon died and Athenion succeeded him.

In 101 the consul Manius Aquillius, Marius' colleague, defeated the rebels and killed Athenion in single combat; he hunted down the remaining bands in 100. The last thousand surrendered on promise of their lives and were sent to Rome to fight wild beasts; they killed each other in the arena instead, the last killing himself.

Diodorus' account, preserved in Byzantine excerpts and derived from Posidonius, is our main source. The war shows the dependence of Sicily's grain estates on slave labour and the violence it generated. It was the second of three great slave revolts in seventy years.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)

set.detail:
The Social War (from socii, allies) was fought between Rome and a confederation of Italian peoples who had long been Rome's allies, providing more than half its armies. Their grievances were exclusion from citizenship and from the rewards of empire, subjection to Roman magistrates' abuses, and the threat to their occupation of public land from the Gracchan reforms. Proposals to enfranchise them by Fulvius Flaccus (125), Gaius Gracchus (122) and Livius Drusus (91) failed; the lex Licinia Mucia of 95 expelled those who had illegally claimed citizenship. Drusus' murder in 91 was the trigger, and the massacre of Romans at Asculum began the war.

The rebels, mainly the Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes and Frentani in the north and the Samnites, Hirpini, Lucanians, Apulians and Campanian towns in the south, created a state, Italia, with its capital at Corfinium, a senate, consuls and coinage. They fielded about 100,000 men, battle-hardened in Roman service. Rome raised a similar number, with Latin, Etruscan, Umbrian, Greek and provincial support. In 90 the rebels won many battles; the consul Rutilius Lupus was killed on the Tolenus. Rome responded with the lex Julia, offering citizenship to loyal allies and those who laid down arms, then the lex Plautia Papiria.

In 89 Rome's armies under Pompeius Strabo, Sulla and Cato regained the initiative. Asculum fell after a long siege, the Marsi surrendered, and Sulla took Pompeii, Stabiae, Aeclanum and Bovianum. By 88 only the Samnites and Lucanians held out, and Nola resisted until 80.

The war cost perhaps 100,000 lives. Its result was the enfranchisement of all Italy south of the Po and the transformation of Rome from a city-state ruling allies into a nation-state, though full integration took decades. It trained the armies and generals of the civil wars.
set.debate: Whether the allies fought for citizenship or independence is the central debate.

scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)

set.detail:
Mithridates VI of Pontus had built an empire around the Black Sea, taking the Crimea, Colchis and Lesser Armenia, and contested Cappadocia and Bithynia with Rome's clients. In 89 the Roman legate Manius Aquillius incited Nicomedes IV of Bithynia to raid Pontus. Mithridates struck back in 88, routing Nicomedes on the Amnias and the Roman forces. Asia welcomed him, and he ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians, the Asiatic Vespers; Aquillius was executed with molten gold. Athens joined him, and his general Archelaus seized Delos and Greece.

Rome was distracted by the Social War and the struggle over the command, which Sulla secured by marching on Rome in 88. He landed in Epirus in 87 with five legions, besieged and sacked Athens and the Piraeus (86), and destroyed Pontic armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenus (86). Meanwhile the Cinnan government sent its own army under Valerius Flaccus, who was murdered by his legate Fimbria; Fimbria defeated Mithridates' son at the Rhyndacus and nearly captured the king at Pitane. Lucullus' fleet won at Tenedos.

Sulla and Mithridates made peace at Dardanus in 85: Mithridates evacuated his conquests, surrendered 70 ships and paid 2,000-3,000 talents, but kept Pontus and was recognised as Rome's ally. Sulla eliminated Fimbria, fined Asia 20,000 talents, and left for Italy in 84.

The war revealed the depth of Greek hatred of Roman exploitation and the vulnerability of the East. Its lenient peace, dictated by Sulla's need to return to Italy, left Mithridates able to fight two more wars. It also made Sulla's army and fortune the instruments of his victory in the civil war.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

set.detail:
The First Sullan Civil War (88-87) began when the tribune Sulpicius Rufus transferred the Mithridatic command from the consul Sulla to Marius. Sulla marched on Rome with six legions, the first time a Roman general had captured the city with a Roman army. Marius fled to Africa; Sulpicius was killed. Sulla passed laws restricting the tribunes and left for Greece, after Cinna, elected consul for 87, swore to respect his acts.

In 87 Cinna revived the proposal to distribute the new citizens through all tribes. His colleague Octavius drove him out of Rome after a battle in the Forum; the Senate deposed him and replaced him with Merula. Cinna won over the army at Nola, raised troops among the new citizens and the Samnites, and recalled Marius, who landed in Etruria. Together with Sertorius and Carbo they besieged Rome, cut off its grain supply, and took it in late 87. The senatorial commander Pompeius Strabo hesitated and died of plague. The victors massacred their enemies, including Octavius, Antonius the orator and two Caesars.

Cinna and Marius were consuls for 86; Marius died days into his seventh consulship. Cinna ruled Rome until 84, holding the consulship four times, with Carbo. His regime enrolled the new citizens in all tribes and passed debt relief, while Sulla fought Mithridates and was declared a public enemy.

The war marked the collapse of the Republic's internal restraints: twice in two years Roman armies took Rome, and political murder became normal. Appian's account sees it as the start of an age of violence. The polarisation between Sullani and Mariani would dominate the next fifty years.

In spring 83 Sulla landed at Brundisium with about 40,000 veterans, determined to overthrow the Cinnan-Marian regime, which had declared him a public enemy. Cinna had been killed by his own troops at Ancona in 84; the government, led by Carbo, the consuls Scipio Asiaticus and Norbanus, and later the younger Marius, mobilised perhaps 100,000 men, including many Samnites and Italians who feared Sulla would reverse their enfranchisement.

In 83 Sulla defeated Norbanus at Mount Tifata and won over Scipio's army near Teanum by negotiation. He was joined by nobles, including Metellus Pius, Crassus and the young Pompey with three private legions from Picenum. In 82 Sulla defeated the younger Marius at Sacriportus, besieging him in Praeneste, and took Rome. In the north, Metellus and Pompey defeated Carbo's generals at Faventia and elsewhere, and Carbo fled to Africa. The Samnites under Pontius Telesinus and Lucanians made a final attack on Rome itself and were destroyed at the Colline Gate on 1 November 82, with thousands of prisoners massacred afterward. Praeneste surrendered; Marius killed himself.

Pompey pursued the remaining Marians to Sicily, where he executed Carbo, and Africa, where he defeated Domitius Ahenobarbus and the Numidian king Iarbas. Sertorius held out in Spain for a decade. Sulla took the dictatorship, proscribed his enemies, devastated Samnium and settled his veterans on confiscated land in Etruria, Campania and Latium.

The war cost tens of thousands of lives and devastated Italy. Its outcome was the Sullan restoration, which tried to make the Senate supreme but was undone within a decade. It made the reputations of Pompey and Crassus.

scholarship: Santangelo, Sulla, the Elites and the Empire (2007)

set.detail:
The Second Mithridatic War (83-81) was a brief, inconclusive conflict provoked by the Roman commander in Asia, Lucius Licinius Murena, whom Sulla had left with Fimbria's two legions. The peace of Dardanus had never been ratified by the Senate. Mithridates was preparing to reconquer the Bosporus and Colchis, which had revolted, and Murena claimed that the king's armaments were aimed at Rome, and that Mithridates had not evacuated all of Cappadocia. Archelaus, Mithridates' former general, who had defected to Rome fearing the king's suspicion, encouraged him.

In 83 Murena invaded Pontic Cappadocia and raided the rich temple city of Comana, plundering the sanctuary of Ma. Mithridates protested to Rome. A Senate envoy, Calidius, told Murena to stop, but apparently without written instructions, and Murena continued his raids in 82, crossing the Halys. Mithridates' general Gordius and then the king himself defeated him decisively on the Halys, and Murena fled to Phrygia. Mithridates expelled the Roman garrisons from Cappadocia.

Sulla, now dictator, sent Aulus Gabinius to order Murena to stop, and to reconcile Mithridates with Ariobarzanes of Cappadocia. Mithridates betrothed his four-year-old daughter to Ariobarzanes and kept part of Cappadocia. Murena nonetheless celebrated a triumph in 81, which Cicero mocked.

The war was a minor affair but showed how Roman commanders in the provinces could provoke wars for personal glory, and how the peace of Dardanus failed to resolve Rome's relations with Pontus. It left Mithridates confident and Rome's position in Anatolia unsettled, preparing the third war in 74.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, a former Sullan who had profited from the proscriptions, was elected consul for 78 against Sulla's wishes, with Pompey's support. After Sulla's death he attacked the dictator's system, proposing to restore the grain dole, recall exiles, return confiscated land to its former owners, and restore the tribunes' powers. He opposed Sulla's state funeral. When dispossessed farmers at Faesulae in Etruria attacked Sullan veterans, the Senate sent both consuls to restore order; Lepidus joined the rebels.

Lepidus refused to return to Rome to hold elections and demanded a second consulship. The Senate, on the urging of Lucius Marcius Philippus, passed the senatus consultum ultimum against him in early 77, entrusting the defence of the state to the proconsul Catulus and to Pompey, who received a special command as a private citizen. Lepidus marched on Rome from Etruria and was defeated by Catulus on the Campus Martius near the Milvian Bridge. His legate in Cisalpine Gaul, Marcus Junius Brutus (father of Caesar's assassin), was besieged by Pompey at Mutina, surrendered and was killed. Lepidus fled to Sardinia, where he died of illness, reportedly grieving over his wife's infidelity.

Perperna took Lepidus' remaining troops, some 20,000, to Spain to join Sertorius. Pompey refused to disband his army and secured the Spanish command as a private citizen.

The rebellion showed the fragility of Sulla's settlement. Lepidus' grievances, the tribunate and land, became the agenda of the 70s. His son Marcus Lepidus was the future triumvir; his other son Lucius Aemilius Paullus was consul in 50.

The Sertorian War (80-72) was the last stand of the Marian cause, fought in Spain by Quintus Sertorius, a Marian general who had gone to Spain in 83 and been driven out in 81. In 80 the Lusitanians invited him back. With a small Roman force and Lusitanian and Celtiberian allies, he defeated a series of Roman commanders and built an alternative Roman state in Spain, with a senate of exiles, magistrates, and a school at Osca for the children of Spanish nobles.

From 79 the proconsul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius campaigned against him in Further Spain with little success, outmanoeuvred by Sertorius' guerrilla tactics, as at Lacobriga. In 77 Perperna brought Lepidus' remnant army, and Pompey received a special command against Sertorius. Pompey crossed the Alps and in 76 was humiliated at Lauro, which Sertorius burned before his eyes; Metellus destroyed Hirtuleius at Italica. In 75 Pompey won at Valentia but was defeated at the Sucro, saved only by Metellus' arrival; the combined armies won at Segontia. Sertorius made an alliance with Mithridates, exchanging Roman officers for money and ships.

From 74 the Romans ground down Sertorian towns in the Ebro valley and Celtiberia. Sertorius grew suspicious and harsh, and in 73 or 72 Perperna murdered him at a banquet at Osca. Pompey crushed Perperna and executed him. The last towns, Uxama, Clunia, Calagurris, fell in 72.

Pompey reorganised Spain, set up his trophy on the Pyrenees, and returned with a large clientele. Sertorius became, in Plutarch and Sallust, a romantic figure, a Roman patriot forced into exile. Archaeology has revealed destruction layers at Valentia and other sites of the war.

scholarship: Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

set.detail:
The Third Mithridatic War began in 74, when Nicomedes IV bequeathed Bithynia to Rome and Mithridates, allied with Sertorius, invaded. He defeated the consul Cotta at Chalcedon but was halted at Cyzicus, where the consul Lucullus besieged the besiegers until famine destroyed the Pontic army (73). Lucullus then conquered Pontus, winning at Cabira (72) and taking Amisus, Sinope and Heraclea, while Mithridates fled to his son-in-law Tigranes II of Armenia.

When Tigranes refused to surrender him, Lucullus invaded Armenia in 69 with a small army, won a famous victory at Tigranocerta, and in 68 defeated the kings again on the Arsanias, but his weary soldiers mutinied near Artaxata, incited by Clodius. Lucullus also restricted the publicani and moneylenders in Asia, making powerful enemies in Rome. Mithridates recovered Pontus and destroyed Triarius' army at Zela (67). Lucullus' provinces were taken from him.

In 66 the lex Manilia gave Pompey the command. He defeated Mithridates at the Lycus, received Tigranes' submission at Artaxata, and pursued the king through the Caucasus, fighting the Albanians and Iberians (65). Mithridates escaped to the Bosporus, where, facing his son Pharnaces' revolt, he died in 63. Pompey annexed Syria, captured Jerusalem, and reorganised the East.

The war was Rome's longest against a foreign enemy in the late Republic. It created the provinces of Bithynia-Pontus and Syria, a ring of client kingdoms, and a vast increase in revenue. It made Pompey the greatest man in Rome and set the stage for the politics of the 60s. Lucullus retired to his gardens and his fish ponds, a byword for luxury.

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

set.detail:
The Third Servile War (73-71) began when some seventy gladiators escaped from a school at Capua, led by the Thracian Spartacus and the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus. They took refuge on Vesuvius, defeated the praetor Glaber by descending the cliffs on vine ladders, and then the praetor Varinius. Slaves and rural poor flocked to them. By 72 their army numbered perhaps 70,000 or more, divided between Spartacus and Crixus, who led a group of Gauls and Germans.

In 72 both consuls, Lucius Gellius and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus, were sent against them. Gellius destroyed Crixus' group at Mount Garganus in Apulia, but Spartacus defeated each consul in turn in Picenum, sacrificed 300 Roman prisoners in honour of Crixus, and marched north, defeating the governor of Cisalpine Gaul, Cassius Longinus, near Mutina. Instead of crossing the Alps, he turned south. The Senate gave Marcus Licinius Crassus, praetor, a special command with six new legions plus the consular armies.

Crassus restored discipline by reviving decimation in a unit that fled. He drove Spartacus into Bruttium, where Cilician pirates failed to ferry him to Sicily, and walled off the peninsula. Spartacus broke out in winter. Crassus destroyed a breakaway group at the Lucanian lake, then defeated and killed Spartacus at the Silarus in spring 71. Six thousand captives were crucified on the Via Appia; Pompey, returning from Spain, killed 5,000 fugitives and claimed credit.

The revolt was the largest slave rising in Roman history and terrified Italy. In modern times Spartacus became a symbol of revolution, from Marx to Kubrick's film. Ancient sources, mostly hostile, nonetheless admired his ability and humanity.

Piracy flourished in the eastern Mediterranean after the decline of Rhodian and Seleucid naval power, encouraged by the demand for slaves at Delos and in Italy, and by Mithridates, who used pirates as allies. The pirates' strongholds were in Rough Cilicia, with its mountainous coast and harbours, and in Crete, but they ranged across the whole Mediterranean, sacking temples, kidnapping travellers for ransom, including the young Caesar in 75, and disrupting trade.

Roman responses were intermittent. In 102 the praetor Marcus Antonius received a command in Cilicia; a law of about 100, known from inscriptions at Delphi and Cnidus, ordered allies to close their ports to pirates. Publius Servilius Vatia campaigned in Lycia, Pamphylia and Isauria from 78 to 74, earning the name Isauricus. In 74 Marcus Antonius Creticus received an extraordinary command over all coasts, but was defeated by the Cretans and died. Quintus Metellus conquered Crete in 69-67. Meanwhile the pirates raided Italy itself, burning a fleet at Ostia, kidnapping praetors, and threatening the grain supply.

In 67 the lex Gabinia gave Pompey command over the entire Mediterranean and coasts for three years, with 500 ships, 120,000 infantry and 24 legates. He divided the sea into thirteen sectors, cleared the western Mediterranean in forty days and Cilicia in forty-nine, winning at Coracesium. He offered surrender on generous terms; some 20,000 pirates were resettled as farmers in depopulated cities such as Soli, renamed Pompeiopolis, and Dyme in Achaea.

The campaign was a model of organisation and clemency. Piracy declined sharply, though it revived during the civil wars under Sextus Pompey. The wars established the precedent of great extraordinary commands that led to the Principate.

scholarship: Ormerod, Piracy in the Ancient World (1924)

set.detail:
Lucius Sergius Catilina, a patrician who had been a Sullan killer, was defeated in the consular elections for 63 and 62. Deeply in debt, he gathered a coalition of bankrupt nobles, ruined Sullan veterans, dispossessed farmers and the urban poor, promising cancellation of debts (novae tabulae). After his defeat in 63 he planned a coup: his ally Gaius Manlius raised an army of veterans and farmers at Faesulae in Etruria, while conspirators in Rome would murder the consul Cicero and set fires.

Cicero, informed through Fulvia, the mistress of a conspirator, obtained the senatus consultum ultimum on 21 October. An attempt on his life on 7 November failed; on 8 November Cicero denounced Catiline in the Senate (the First Catilinarian), and Catiline left Rome to join Manlius. In December the conspirators led by the praetor Lentulus Sura approached envoys of the Allobroges, who reported to Cicero; their arrest at the Milvian Bridge with incriminating letters exposed the plot. On 5 December, after the debate between Caesar and Cato, the Senate voted death, and five conspirators were executed in the Tullianum.

Catiline's army, about 12,000 men but only a quarter properly armed, tried to escape to Gaul but was trapped in the Apennines between Metellus Celer and the consul Antonius. In January 62 at Pistoria (Pistoia), Marcus Petreius, commanding for Antonius, who pleaded gout, destroyed it. Catiline died fighting at the front, found far ahead of his men, still breathing.

Sallust's Bellum Catilinae and Cicero's speeches made the conspiracy one of the most famous episodes of Roman history. Modern historians debate whether it was a revolutionary movement, a desperate coup by a bankrupt aristocrat, or exaggerated by Cicero for political gain.

Caesar's Gallic War (58-50) brought Gaul between the Pyrenees, the Rhine and the Atlantic under Roman control. In 58 he blocked the Helvetian migration at Geneva and destroyed it at Bibracte, then defeated Ariovistus' Germans in Alsace. In 57 he crushed the Belgic coalition at the Axona and the Nervii at the Sabis, and his legates received the submission of Armorica. In 56 he destroyed the Veneti in a naval battle in Quiberon Bay, while Publius Crassus conquered Aquitania. In 55 he massacred the Usipetes and Tencteri, bridged the Rhine and made his first expedition to Britain; in 54 he crossed again with five legions and forced Cassivellaunus to submit.

In winter 54/53 the Eburones under Ambiorix destroyed fifteen cohorts at Atuatuca, and other tribes rose; Caesar suppressed them in 53 with savage devastation. In 52 the Arvernian Vercingetorix led a general revolt. Caesar took Avaricum, was repulsed at Gergovia, and finally besieged Vercingetorix at Alesia, defeating a vast relief army. In 51 he and his legates subdued the last resistance, culminating at Uxellodunum, where the defenders' hands were cut off.

Plutarch, from Caesar's own figures, says he took 800 towns, subdued 300 peoples, fought three million men, killing a million and enslaving another million. The figures are inflated but suggest the scale. The war enriched Caesar and his army, created a loyal veteran force of ten legions, and gave Caesar military glory rivalling Pompey's.

Caesar's Commentarii, seven books plus Hirtius' eighth, are our main source, a masterpiece of self-presentation. The conquest added a vast and rich province, organised by Augustus into three provinces, and began the Romanisation of northern Europe. Modern scholars debate the morality, the numbers, and the extent to which Caesar provoked the war.
set.debate: Casualty and population figures are much disputed; recent work treats the conquest as including episodes of genocide.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome, obtained the province of Syria for five years by the lex Trebonia of 55, intending a war against Parthia that would give him military glory to match Pompey's and Caesar's. There was no clear casus belli: Parthia was divided by a succession struggle between the brothers Orodes II and Mithridates IV, and Gabinius, Crassus' predecessor, had intervened briefly. The tribune Ateius Capito cursed Crassus as he left Rome in November 55.

In 54 Crassus crossed the Euphrates, occupied Greek cities in Mesopotamia, and withdrew to winter in Syria, where he plundered the temples of Jerusalem and Hierapolis. His son Publius joined him with 1,000 Gallic cavalry.
