In 53 he crossed again with seven legions and marched across the desert toward Seleucia, rejecting the advice of Artavasdes of Armenia to go through the mountains. Near Carrhae the Suren's 10,000 cavalry, horse archers resupplied by camel trains and armoured cataphracts, destroyed his army. Publius was killed; Crassus retreated and was killed during a parley. Twenty thousand Romans died, ten thousand were captured, and the legionary standards were lost.

Gaius Cassius Longinus, Crassus' quaestor, escaped with 500 cavalry, organised the defence of Syria and in 51 repulsed a Parthian invasion under Pacorus near Antigonea. Bibulus, the new governor, sat out the threat in Antioch.

Carrhae was one of Rome's greatest defeats, a trauma that shaped its eastern policy for decades: Caesar planned a war of revenge, Antony attempted one in 36, and Augustus finally recovered the standards by diplomacy in 20 BC. It also broke the triumvirate, leaving Caesar and Pompey to confront each other.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
Caesar's civil war (49-45) arose from the failure to agree on the terms of his return from Gaul. Fearing prosecution if he became a private citizen, Caesar demanded to stand for a second consulship in absence; his enemies, now allied with Pompey, insisted he lay down his command first. After the senatus consultum ultimum of 7 January 49, Caesar crossed the Rubicon with one legion. Italy fell within weeks; Pompey and the consuls evacuated to Greece from Brundisium. Caesar took Corfinium, pardoning Domitius Ahenobarbus, seized the treasury, and defeated Pompey's legates in Spain at Ilerda; Massilia fell after a siege, but Curio was killed in Africa.

In 48 Caesar crossed to Epirus. He blockaded Pompey at Dyrrachium but was defeated, retreated to Thessaly, and destroyed Pompey's army at Pharsalus on 9 August. Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered. Caesar, pursuing him, became involved in the Alexandrian War and the affair with Cleopatra; in 47 he defeated Pharnaces at Zela.

The Pompeians regrouped in Africa under Metellus Scipio, Cato, Labienus and Juba; Caesar defeated them at Thapsus in April 46, and Cato killed himself at Utica. Pompey's sons raised Spain; Caesar defeated them at Munda in March 45, his hardest battle.

The war was fought across the Mediterranean. Caesar's clemency toward defeated Romans contrasted with Sulla's proscriptions and won him support, though many pardoned enemies later joined his assassination. The war ended in Caesar's dictatorship and monarchy. Our sources include Caesar's own Civil War, the continuators of the Alexandrian, African and Spanish Wars, Cicero's letters, Lucan's epic, Plutarch, Appian and Dio.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

set.detail:
The Alexandrian War (October 48 to March 47) began when Caesar, arriving in Alexandria in pursuit of Pompey with only 4,000 men, tried to arbitrate the dynastic conflict between Ptolemy XIII and his sister Cleopatra VII, as executor of their father's will, and demanded repayment of debts owed to him. He favoured Cleopatra after she came to him secretly. The regent Pothinus and general Achillas, with the Alexandrian population and 20,000 soldiers, including veterans of Gabinius' army, besieged Caesar in the palace quarter.

Caesar held a small area by the harbour, burned the Egyptian fleet (the fire possibly damaging book stores), and seized the Pharos. Arsinoe IV, Cleopatra's younger sister, escaped to the Egyptian army and had Achillas killed; her eunuch Ganymedes took command and tried to poison Caesar's water supply with seawater. A naval battle and fighting over the Heptastadion mole followed, in which Caesar had to swim to safety. Caesar released Ptolemy XIII, who joined his army.

Relief came in spring 47 from Mithridates of Pergamon, with an army from Syria and Cilicia and 3,000 Jews under Antipater, who stormed Pelusium. Caesar joined them, and at the battle of the Nile in March 47 the Egyptian army was destroyed; Ptolemy XIII drowned. Caesar made Cleopatra queen with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV, left three legions in Egypt, and sent Arsinoe to Rome.

The war delayed Caesar for months, allowing the Pompeians to regroup in Africa and Pharnaces to invade Pontus. It began his relationship with Cleopatra and her role in Roman politics. The Bellum Alexandrinum, probably by Hirtius, is the main narrative.

scholarship: Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)

set.detail:
The War of Mutina (44-43) was the Senate's attempt, led by Cicero, to crush Mark Antony after Caesar's death. In June 44 Antony, as consul, had a law passed giving him Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul for five years, in place of Macedonia, and recalled the legions from Macedonia. Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins and governor of Cisalpine Gaul under Caesar's arrangements, refused to hand over his province. In November two legions defected from Antony to Octavian, who had raised a private army. Antony marched north and besieged Decimus in Mutina in December 44.

In Rome Cicero delivered the Philippics, urging war. In January 43 the Senate gave Octavian propraetorian imperium and sent the consuls Hirtius and Pansa with Octavian to relieve Mutina, after a failed embassy to Antony. Antony was declared a public enemy. On 14 April at Forum Gallorum Antony mauled Pansa's recruits, but was defeated by Hirtius; Pansa died of his wounds. On 21 April Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's lines at Mutina; Hirtius was killed, but Antony withdrew over the Alps with his remaining forces.

The victory proved hollow. With both consuls dead, the Senate gave command to Decimus Brutus, slighting Octavian. Lepidus, Plancus and Pollio, governors in the west, joined Antony; Decimus was abandoned and killed. Octavian marched on Rome, took the consulship in August, and in November allied with Antony and Lepidus at Bononia.

The war marked Cicero's last great political effort and the Senate's last attempt to control the Caesarian generals. Its failure led directly to the Second Triumvirate and the proscriptions, in which Cicero died.

The Liberators' civil war (43-42) pitted the triumvirs Antony and Octavian against Caesar's assassins, Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius. After leaving Italy in 44, Brutus took Macedonia and Greece, raising legions from Caesarian veterans and recruits, while Cassius seized Syria, absorbing the armies of Caecilius Bassus and others, besieged Dolabella at Laodicea, and forced the cities of Asia to contribute vast sums. The lex Pedia of August 43 condemned them; the triumvirate, formed in November, prepared to fight them.

In 42 Cassius took Rhodes and Brutus sacked Xanthus in Lycia, where the inhabitants killed themselves rather than surrender. The two met at Sardis and marched to Macedonia with nineteen legions, taking a strong position at Philippi astride the Via Egnatia, with their fleet controlling the sea. Antony and Octavian crossed with nineteen legions, short of supplies.

In the first battle of Philippi, in October 42, Antony took Cassius' camp while Brutus took Octavian's; Cassius, wrongly thinking all lost, killed himself. On the same day the Liberators' fleet destroyed triumviral reinforcements at sea. Three weeks later, pressed by his officers, Brutus gave battle and was defeated; he killed himself. Many nobles died or surrendered.

The victory gave the triumvirs control of the empire. Antony took the East, Octavian returned to Italy to settle veterans, and Lepidus was marginalised. For many Romans, Philippi marked the death of the Republic. The Liberators' coinage, including the EID MAR denarius, documents their claims. The survivors, including Messalla and Horace, eventually joined the victors.
